  "chapter_body_excerpt": "## 12 Punish, but how? Mad acts and their punishments, 1750-1911 Chapter 11 explained why most killings committed because of insanity between 1669 and 1750 were sentenced under a law called “killing because of madness,” which requested that killers pay a monetary compensation to the family of their victims. In the second half of the eighteenth century, however, death sentences became common for the same acts, while ever stricter measures of preventive confinement were imposed on “people with madness illness.” By 1850, nine sub-statutes discussed mad homicides, and an increasing number of “circulars” (通行) and “memoranda” (説貼) from the Ministry of Punishments instructed legal officials on how to handle these crimes. Why were so many different punishments imposed for homicides that used to be sentenced in the same way until the 1750s? The diverse sentences meted out for killings committed “because of madness” did not reflect Chinese ambiguities about the criminal responsibility of mad people, but changing assessments of the justness of sentencing in specific cases. Although the legal view of mad acts did not change, the insanity of killers was no longer the only circumstance deemed relevant to sentencing. The diversity of punishments resulted from unsystematic attempts by Qing officials to impose severe punishments for acts that led to grave outcomes, and to maintain equilibrium between the penalties required for proximate crimes. The reporting of such cases by palace memorial explains the apparent surge of cases of mad parenticide that took place in the 1760s and 70s. I have found 17 cases from 1766 to 1777 in the Grand Council archives (LFZZ; the date of the report and the identity of the victim are indicated in parentheses): mf 087.1413 (QL31.9.22; father), mf 087.1433 (QL31.10.6; mother), mf 087.1479 (QL32.2.6; father), mf 087.1506 (QL32.6.29; mother), mf 087.1588 (QL33.5.26; mother), mf 087.1614 (QL33.7.6; father), mf 087.1620 (QL33.7.8; mother), mf 087.1655 (QL33.9.28; father), mf 087.1663 (QL33.11.26; “stepmother” 繼母), mf 087.1886 (QL38.9.18; father), mf 097.1112 (QL39.3.16; mother), mf 097.1285 (QL39.5.24; mother), mf 087.2284 (QL41.5.29; mother), mf 087.2341 (QL41.7.26; father’s sister 親姑), mf 087.2465 (QL42.4.18; father), mf 087.2636 (QL42.4.25; mother). The Daoguang emperor (r. 1821-1850) adopted the same approach as Qianlong. In 1823, an imperial edict was turned into a law mandating that the crime of “striking one’s parents to death” should be sentenced to death by dismemberment regardless of whether madness was involved.
